title: nibli: the LLM drafts, the engine decides
respell: Dhilip Siva dot dev, slash nibli playground

sentences.show: Language models predict the next word. A reasoner derives the next step.
In five minutes: what symbolic reasoning is, what a theorem prover does, where an LLM fits around one, and a small proof in nibli, step by step.
Symbolic reasoning works on explicit statements and explicit rules.
Here are three: every dog is an animal, every animal eats, and Adam is a dog.
Nothing is learned from examples, and nothing is guessed.
A conclusion counts only if it follows from these statements by fixed rules of inference.
Run it again tomorrow and you get the same answer, and you can inspect every step that produced it.
A theorem prover automates that.
You give it premises and a claim, and it searches for a proof: a chain of rule applications from the premises to the claim.
If it finds one, the answer is TRUE, and it can show you the chain.
That answer is sound with respect to what you encoded.
It doesn't make your premises true. It tells you what they commit you to.
nibli answers with one of four verdicts: TRUE; FALSE, meaning not derivable; UNKNOWN, with a reason; and RESOURCE_EXCEEDED, when a depth, fuel or memory budget runs out.

sentences.show: A neuro-symbolic system pairs a neural front end with a symbolic core, and lets each do what it's good at.
Language models are good at reading prose.
So in nibli, an LLM can formalize plain English into nibli KR, the engine's rule language.
That draft sits outside the reasoning firewall.
Before anything reasons over it, deterministic gates check it.
The grammar. A committed vocabulary, where an unknown word is an error instead of a guess. The semantic compiler. And a round trip back to canonical text.
Then a person reviews the rules and their back-translation: a fixed, mechanical reading, with no model involved.
This example comes pre-encoded, so the Formalize button is switched off and we skip the drafting.
The LLM drafts. The engine decides.
nibli is the engine I build in Rust.
It's a theorem prover, and it's open source.
It compiles nibli KR into first-order logic, and answers claims by backward chaining over a fact store.
The whole pipeline, parser, compiler and reasoner, runs right here in the browser as WebAssembly, and also under Wasmtime or as a native crate.
It never invents a fact, a rule or a proof step.
Here's the syllogism example: three lines of nibli KR.
The first reads: for every X, if X is a dog, then X is an animal.
The second: for every X, if X is an animal, then X eats.
The third: Adam is a dog.
We don't ask a question. We state the claim to check: Adam eats.
The engine starts from the claim and works backward.
The goal is: Adam eats. No stored fact says so.
So it looks for a rule whose conclusion is eats: line two, every animal eats.
Matching that conclusion to the goal binds X to Adam, and leaves a new goal: Adam is an animal.
Again there's no stored fact, so it looks for a rule that concludes animal: line one, every dog is an animal.
That leaves one goal, Adam is a dog, and that one is stored.
The chain closes in two rule steps.
To find the shortest chain, the engine first runs a cheap search without recording, raising the depth limit one step at a time until the claim resolves.
Then it runs the search once more at that depth, this time recording every step. That record is the proof trace.
The stored fact becomes a leaf, marked given.
Each rule step becomes a node that cites the source line it used.
“Adam eats” cites recorded source #1: every animal eats.
“Adam is an animal” cites recorded source #0: every dog is an animal.
Open the role-level detail, and you see what those lines are made of.
The fact is stored as an event with named roles: the dog, Adam, and a breed nobody specified.
When the same sub-goal comes up again, the trace says “proved above” and points back, instead of proving it twice.
The playground folds the whole record into the three lines you saw, with a plain-English why.
Now the claim that Adam is a bird.
Nothing in the knowledge base supports it, so the answer is FALSE.
The why line says no example could be found that satisfies the claim.
Here, FALSE means not derivable from what we asserted. It isn't a proof that Adam isn't a bird.
nibli won't claim more than its premises support.
Try it at dhilipsiva.dev/nibli-playground. The code is on GitHub.
It's also the running example in my book, Ultimate Neuro-Symbolic Reasoning for AI Engineers, scheduled for December 2026.
I'm dhilipsiva.
